lead: Learning types differ by the feedback a learner receives. Supervised learning gets labelled examples, so it learns a mapping from input to known answer. Unsupervised learning gets only inputs and looks for structure such as groups. Reinforcement learning gets a reward after actions, often delayed. This choice sets the data you need, the loss you use and how you judge success. IRCTC waitlist prediction, UPI fraud checks, crop grouping and game-playing agents are everyday places where the three types appear.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for task, data and model terms.

sections.h3: Supervised learning: labels give the answer

blocks.text: Supervised learning uses pairs (x, y). x is the input vector, called features. y is the target, called the label. The learner searches for a function f that predicts y from x. At test time a new x arrives without y, and f(x) gives the prediction. The labels make the error measurable, so training can adjust f to reduce mistakes.

blocks.where: y is the target; x is the feature vector; f is the learned model; ε is noise or error not explained by x.

blocks.text: If y is discrete, the task is classification. Example: from 200 labelled emails, predict spam or not spam. If y is a number, the task is regression. Example: predict house price in rupees from area in square feet. The same features can support either task; the type of y decides the name.

items: Classification output: class label, such as spam/not spam, confirmed/waitlisted.
Regression output: real number, such as price or waiting-list position.
Training data must be labelled; wrong labels teach wrong rules.

blocks.text: A typical supervised pipeline is: collect labelled examples, split into train and test, fit the model on train, tune with validation, report test error. Details of regression, logistic regression, trees and SVM come in Units 2 and 3.

Unsupervised learning uses inputs x only. No y is given, so the learner cannot measure a prediction error against a correct answer. It looks for structure: groups of similar points, low-dimensional directions, or a probability distribution that could have produced the data.

Clustering puts points into groups so that points in one group are more similar to each other than to points outside. Example: group 500 customers by monthly spend and visit frequency. The bank may name the groups later, but the algorithm only sees features. Density estimation models how data is distributed; it can flag a UPI transaction as unusual if it lies in a low-density region.

items: Clustering: hard or soft group assignment; number of groups may be chosen by the analyst.
Density estimation: a model p(x) over inputs; useful for anomaly detection.
No labels means no single correct answer; evaluation uses separation, stability or domain review.

blocks.text: A typical pipeline is: choose features, scale them, pick a similarity or distance, run the method, inspect groups. Unit 4 covers k-means, hierarchical clustering, Gaussian mixtures and PCA. Some syllabi call semi-supervised learning a mix: a few labels plus many unlabelled inputs. Self-supervised learning makes labels from the data itself, such as predicting the next word.

Reinforcement learning (RL) trains an agent that acts in an environment. At each step the agent sees a state s, chooses an action a, and receives a reward r plus the next state. The reward is a number, not a correct action label. The agent must discover which actions lead to high total reward over time. The agent's policy is its rule for choosing actions.

Feedback is delayed. A cricket shot may score runs only after the ball reaches the boundary; a robot gets +1 only when it exits the maze. The agent explores actions to learn, then exploits good actions. This trade-off between exploration and exploitation is central.

items: Choose action a, sometimes random for exploration.
Receive reward r and next state s′.
Update the estimate of how good each action is, or the policy, from the reward.
Repeat until the run ends; test the learned policy.

blocks.text: Example: teach a robot to exit a maze with +1 at the exit and 0 elsewhere. The agent is the robot; states are cell positions; actions are up/down/left/right; reward is +1 on exit. Unit 6 covers Q-learning and related methods.

figure.caption: The tree splits machine learning by feedback: labels for supervised, no labels for unsupervised, and reward for reinforcement. Notice that classification and regression sit under supervised learning because both use labels.

spec.aria: A tree with machine learning at the root and three branches: supervised learning with classification and regression, unsupervised learning with clustering, and reinforcement learning with an agent.

examples.question: Classify each task as supervised classification, supervised regression, unsupervised clustering or reinforcement learning. Also count how many tasks fall in each of the three broad types. (1) Predict house price from area. (2) Group 500 customers by monthly spend. (3) Teach a robot to exit a maze using +1 at the exit. (4) Label email spam from 200 labelled examples. (5) Find clusters in 1000 UPI transactions. (6) Choose a cricket shot using runs scored as reward.
steps: Task 1: target is house price, a number in rupees. The label is numeric, so this is supervised regression.
Task 2: no target label; input is monthly spend. Grouping customers by similarity is unsupervised clustering.
Task 3: the robot takes actions and gets +1 at the exit. Reward is delayed, not a labelled correct action, so this is reinforcement learning.
Task 4: target is spam/not spam, a discrete label, with 200 labelled examples. This is supervised classification.
Task 5: no labels on UPI transactions; the goal is to find groups. This is unsupervised clustering.
Task 6: a cricket shot is chosen; runs scored is a reward signal. This is reinforcement learning.
Count: supervised = tasks 1 and 4 = 2. Unsupervised = tasks 2 and 5 = 2. Reinforcement = tasks 3 and 6 = 2.
examples.answer: Tasks 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 are supervised regression, unsupervised clustering, reinforcement learning, supervised classification, unsupervised clustering and reinforcement learning; the counts are 2 supervised, 2 unsupervised and 2 reinforcement.
examples.check:
tasks = [
    ('Predict house price from area', 'supervised'),
    ('Group 500 customers by monthly spend', 'unsupervised'),
    ('Teach a robot to exit a maze using +1 at the exit', 'reinforcement'),
    ('Label email spam from 200 labelled examples', 'supervised'),
    ('Find clusters in 1000 UPI transactions', 'unsupervised'),
    ('Choose a cricket shot using runs scored as reward', 'reinforcement'),
]
for kind in ['supervised', 'unsupervised', 'reinforcement']:
    print(sum(1 for _, label in tasks if label == kind))

traps: Clustering is not classification. Classification needs labels; clustering only has inputs and finds groups.
Reinforcement learning uses rewards, not labelled correct actions. A reward tells how good an action was, not what the action should have been.
Regression predicts a number; classification predicts a class. A price in rupees is regression even if you later bucket it.
Unsupervised does not mean unvalidated. You still check cluster stability, separation or business meaning.
Semi-supervised is not unsupervised. It uses a small labelled set plus a large unlabelled set.

quiz.q: Name the three broad learning types and the feedback each uses.
quiz.a: Supervised uses labels, unsupervised uses no labels, and reinforcement uses reward.

quiz.q: Why can a supervised learner measure training error but an unsupervised learner cannot measure a label error?
quiz.a: Supervised data has y, so prediction f(x) can be compared with the true y. Unsupervised data has no y, so there is no label to compare against.

quiz.q: A dataset has 10,000 UPI transactions with no fraud labels. You group them by amount and time. Which learning type is this, and what is the main evaluation difficulty?
quiz.a: This is unsupervised clustering. With no labels there is no single correct grouping, so evaluation needs separation, stability or domain review.

quiz.q: A team says it will use classification to predict tomorrow's temperature in °C. Is that correct? What should it be?
quiz.a: It is not correct. Temperature in °C is a continuous number, so the task is regression. Classification predicts a discrete class.

quiz.q: In reinforcement learning, define agent, state, action and reward.
quiz.a: The agent is the learner or decision maker. State is the current situation. Action is a choice the agent makes. Reward is a number received after an action.

quiz.q: Why is delayed reward harder than a supervised label?
quiz.a: A label tells the correct answer immediately. A delayed reward may arrive many steps later, so the agent must work out which earlier actions helped or hurt.

quiz.q: Classify: (a) predict waitlist confirmation from PNR features with 5,000 labelled cases; (b) group crops by rainfall and soil.
quiz.a: (a) Supervised classification, because the label is discrete and labelled cases exist. (b) Unsupervised clustering, because there are no labels and the aim is to form groups.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern systems often mix the three types: self-supervised pretraining on text, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback. Recommendation engines combine unsupervised grouping with supervised click prediction. Search for self-supervised learning, RLHF, and semi-supervised learning if you want the extensions.
